Celts weren't a single homogenous group. The original (Central European) Hallstatt and La Tene cultures were, but otherwise the other Celtic cultures were tribes that either mixed with the original Celts, or simply adopted their culture (most likely mixed though). Gauls were probably both, depending on where in France we're talking. Northern French tribes were obviously Germanic, but France is a big place, and your average Frenchman is certainly darker haired than a Scandinavian. Spain was a mix, with Celts settling in the northwest, and mixing with the Iberians to the southeast. British Isles Insular Celts are definitely native populations mixed with Continental Celts. Anglo-Saxons came later.

Most Celts, like most modern Europeans, ended up a mix of Early European Farmer (EEF), Ancient North Eurasian (ANE), and Western Hunter Gatherer (WHG). The differences in Europeans are caused by the varying degrees of admixture of these three racial groups. Nordics are high in ANE and WHG, but low in EEF. Hence blonde hair and blue eyes (and why some consider only Northern Europeans white). Southern Europeans are high in EEF, and have some to little WHG and ANE. Hence a darker, more swarthy look. Sardinians are pretty much entirely EEF.

Europe was originally largely populated by WHGs during the Paleolithic Era. In the early Neolithic, EEFs came out of Anatolia and mixed with the native population, mostly in the south. The further north you went, the less EEF admixture. In the late Neolithic, ANEs (these were the Indo-Europeans) came out of the Eurasian Steppe and mixed with the European populations, mostly in Central and especially Northern Europe. This is the exact cause of the north/south divide in genetics in Europe and applies to both Western and Eastern populations.
